Power in literature is the central mechanism of conflict: the ability to shape the world, compel obedience, and determine others' fates. Works exploring power ask whether it corrupts, whether it validates or destroys the wielder, and whether it can ever be wielded justly. From Macbeth's grab for the Scottish throne to King Lear's abdication and Othello's paranoia, power reveals character at the breaking point.

The pursuit of power drives tragedy. There is ambition to seize it, paranoia to keep it, and guilt for having seized it through murder or manipulation. Power over others necessitates power over oneself. The tyrant is undone by his own desires, and the king is destroyed by his own rage. Illegitimate power—usurped crowns and stolen authority—generates supernatural consequences or inevitable reckoning, as in Macbeth. The constraints on power—law, custom, morality, and conscience—define what separates the ruler from the despot. Their violation marks the descent into tragedy.

Power corrupts judgment. The powerful character misreads flattery as loyalty in King Lear, mistakes suggestion for fact in Othello, or rationalizes murder as necessity in Macbeth. Powerlessness and subjection are not passive states. They generate their own interior dramas—revenge, madness, moral resistance—as in characters like Edmund and Iago. Literary power is often represented as corrupting when unquestioned. The presence of counsel, conscience, or rival power creates moral tension. The dissolution of power reveals truth. When the powerful fall—deposed, exiled, or mad—what they have hidden becomes visible and tragic: their fragility, their dependence on others, their humanity.

Power is often visualized through objects: crowns, thrones, scepters, and kingdoms themselves. Control of these objects is both symbolic and material. Losing them is both metaphorical death and literal dispossession. Ambition becomes the desire for power and the psychological engine of the tragic drive. Authority provides the legitimacy that sustains power. Questioned authority unravels the ruler's stability. Kingship represents the supreme concentration of power in one mortal body and the test of whether humans can bear such weight. Macbeth stands as the archetype of power seized and power corrupted, where murder for the crown destroys the murderer. King Lear explores the abdication of power and its consequences, where dispossession becomes tragedy. Othello shows power undermined by manipulation, with the military commander destroyed by private jealousy. Tragedy itself uses power as its engine: the fall of the powerful or the powerless crushed beneath power.
